name: Remoir synthetic pipeline evaluation set v1
description: Questions over four SYNTHETIC fixture documents generated by scripts/make_fixtures.py. The documents are fictional and exist only to test the software pipeline; results on this set say nothing about performance on real academic papers.
relevance_procedure: Labels were written by hand from the fixture source text in scripts/make_fixtures.py. Each relevant item is (document, PDF page, evidence phrase). A retrieved chunk is relevant to an item if it comes from that document and contains the evidence phrase (case-insensitive substring). Labels do not depend on chunk ids, so they stay valid when chunking settings change.

questions.question: What methodology did the authors of the maize rainfall study use?
questions.reference_answer: A panel fixed-effects regression with district and year fixed effects, combining district yield records with daily rainfall from 118 stations.

questions.question: How was rainfall variability measured?

relevant.evidence: coefficient of variation of daily rainfall

questions.reference_answer: As the coefficient of variation of daily rainfall during the growing season.

questions.question: What limitations did the researchers of the maize rainfall study identify?
questions.reference_answer: Self-reported yields, sparse stations in the north, no pests or soil degradation, a short time window.

questions.question: What evidence supports the conclusion that rainfall variability affects crop yields?
questions.reference_answer: An 11.4 percent yield decline per SD of variability, and 1.8 percent loss per extra dry day during flowering.

questions.question: How much did irrigation reduce the impact of rainfall variability on maize?
questions.reference_answer: Irrigated districts declined 5.9 percent per SD versus 11.4 percent in rain-fed districts.

questions.question: Which machine learning model performed best for crop yield prediction?

relevant.evidence: gradient boosting achieved the lowest error

questions.reference_answer: Gradient boosting (RMSE 0.42 t/ha).

questions.question: How did the machine learning study avoid data leakage?
questions.reference_answer: By training on 2005-2016 and testing on 2017-2019 (temporal split).

questions.question: What was the strongest predictor of crop yields in the machine learning study?
questions.reference_answer: Mid-season vegetation index (NDVI).

questions.question: What are the limitations of the machine learning yield models?
questions.reference_answer: Single-country training data, cloud cover, no extreme drought years in testing.

questions.question: How can machine learning be applied in agriculture?
questions.reference_answer: Yield forecasts for food security planning, insurance pricing and fertilizer distribution.

questions.question: What do the documents say about ecosystem services?

relevant.evidence: pollination, soil fertility, water regulation and carbon storage

questions.reference_answer: Agricultural landscapes provide pollination, soil fertility, water regulation and carbon storage.

questions.question: How much semi-natural habitat supports higher pollinator diversity?
questions.reference_answer: At least twenty percent semi-natural habitat.

questions.question: What research gaps are identified across the uploaded documents?
questions.reference_answer: Economic value of ecosystem services, few long-term and tropical studies; long-term impact evaluation with randomised trials.

questions.question: How do healthy soils help crops cope with rainfall variability?
questions.reference_answer: They retain moisture and buffer crops against dry spells.

questions.question: What evidence about climate change does the policy brief provide?
questions.reference_answer: Temperatures up 1.2 C since 1980 and a rainy season about nine days shorter.

questions.question: Why does the policy brief not recommend large irrigation schemes?
questions.reference_answer: They cost about 9,000 dollars per hectare and are not cost-effective for most smallholders.

questions.question: What data did the policy brief's recommendations draw on?
questions.reference_answer: 23 household surveys with 1,450 farmers and interviews with extension officers.

questions.question: Which uncertainties does the policy brief report?

relevant.evidence: climate projections for rainfall in the region disagree

questions.reference_answer: Disagreeing rainfall projections, low insurance uptake, possible overstatement in surveys.

questions.question: Do the documents disagree about whether rainfall variability affects maize yields?
questions.reference_answer: Yes: the rainfall study finds strong negative effects, the ML study finds variability adds no predictive power for maize.

questions.question: Compare the limitations reported by the maize rainfall study and the machine learning study.
questions.reference_answer: Rainfall study: data quality and coverage; ML study: transferability, cloud cover, no drought years.

questions.question: Do the documents agree on irrigation as a way to adapt to climate risk?
questions.reference_answer: Partly not: the rainfall study finds irrigation buffers losses; the brief calls large schemes not cost-effective.

questions.question: How many weather stations provided rainfall data for the maize study?
questions.reference_answer: 118 weather stations.

questions.question: What effect did drought-tolerant seed have on yields?
questions.reference_answer: Adopters reported 18 percent higher dry-season yields in 2022.

questions.question: Why is weather-index insurance uptake low?
questions.reference_answer: Premiums are unaffordable for the poorest households.
